Life in the heart of centres 


The Montreal YMCA is a partnership of volunteers and staff committed to the fulfillment of people 
in spirit, mind and body and to the development of self-reliance in the individual and the community. 


Through its actions, programs and services, the Montreal YMCA reflects the needs and aspirations 
of the communities and works with individuals, local communities and communities in developing 
countries in achieving social justice and control of their environments.”

Message from the Chair of the Board of Directors 
and the President and the Chief Executive Officer 


Montreal YMCA 


The Montreal YMCA maintained its momentum, which began with the campaign to revitalize the 
Downtown YMCA in the year 2000. The dynamic and open attitude that prevailed during the year 
throughout our association, combined with the sound financial position passed on by our 
predecessors have enabled us to make a smooth transition with senior management. 


Guided by the main orientations and objectives set out in our Vision 2005 plan, all of the association's 
centres undertook a strategic planning exercise, which will enable them to ensure their long-term 
viability and establish clear orientations that address the specific needs of their respective 
communities. In addition, we have continued to renovate our facilities and expand our programs and 
services within and outside our walls. We have also conducted studies and consultations to evaluate 
the possibility of offering targeted programs and services in areas where we are not represented, 
especially off the Island of Montreal. 


Since our increased influence is for the most part supported by our staff and adulii 
volunteers, we have also invested significantly in training and support for our #a 
human resources. 


The results prove that we were on the right track. As you will see when 
reading about some of our accomplishments, our centres have shown that ry 
the physical limits of their space in no way limits their innovative spirit as 

they continue to form partnerships with other institutions in their communities. 


Our influence in the field has earned us some excellent coverage in the print and electronic media. 
The YMCA is in the process of becoming a top source for the media on community life in Montreal. 
There is obviously strong interest in what we do as evidenced by the coverage of activities, such as 
the CD Y5550, First Stop program and Cleanup Rally. 


We wish to thank all staff and volunteers, because they are so dedicated and generous with their time 
and energy. Thanks to them, the Montreal YMCA is ending this fiscal year as an organization that is 
more effective and more present than ever. 


Suzanne Aboud Stéphane Vaillancourt 


Chair of the Board of Directors President and Chief Executive 
Officer 


Life in the heart of centres 


DOWNTOWN YMCA - WHEN COMPASSION TURNS INTO ACTION 
When J. Gregorio was forced to flee Venezuela with his wife and two children in December 2002, they arrived 
in Montreal without any money or contacts. The only thing they had was their fear. 


“The YMCA was like an oasis in the middle of the desert for us. The Residence offered us a heated room and 
good meals. Staff members were all very kind. Employees at SARIMM (a Montreal-based organization that 
provides assistance to refugees and immigrants) and the Covered Garden put us in touch with the various 
government services. They gave us what a refugee needs most: understanding. My family and I will always be 
very grateful to the YMCA. They put the first roof over our heads and were our first family in Canada.” 


Bernadette left a war-torn African country. With the assistance of Immigration Services, she arrived in 
Montreal, where she was welcomed by SARIMM and directed to the YMCA Residence. She stayed there from 
June 16 to July 2, 2003. “They offered me accommodation and three solid meals a day. And they listened to 
me. The staff helped me with the preliminary steps for obtaining the right to permanent resident status in 
Canada. For someone like me who comes from a country torn apart by hatred, I was impressed by the warm 
welcome I received from the people at the YMCA. Although the war separated me from my children, I was 
comforted by the YMCA’s approach with youth. The whole experience made me decide to contribute to the 
YMCA’s work by becoming a volunteer.” 


Gregorio and Bernadette are among the 3,570 asylum seekers who stayed at the YMCA last year. 


DU PARC YMCA - SCHOOL GOES 3D 

The Montreal YMCA had only just announced the goal of extending its services outside its centres when the 
Du Parc YMCA sprang into action. The centre joined forces with the Saint-Louis high school to explore new 
ways to help youth succeed at the academic, social and personal levels. Their efforts led to the creation of 
the CAFE 3D (“3D” is short for the French words développement, découverte et détente — development, 
discovery and relaxation), a place at school where youth get together to relax, featuring a pool table, soccer 
table, board games, video games, etc. Youth also organize social, community, cultural and sports projects and 
activities. Other partners joined in, including community kitchens, which offer cooking workshops to youth, 
and the CHAFRIQ, which organizes sports tournaments. 


The project proved successful before long. Four youth, backed by the entire Café 3D team, participated in the 
Secondaires en spectacle contest, a first for the school. The school principal says that the café is now at the 
centre of a good number of projects and activities in the school. 


GUY-FAVREAU YMCA - SCHOOL SUPPLIES, EASTER EGGS AND MORE 
Volunteers and staff at the Guy-Favreau centre look after local youth with uncommon generosity and 
openness. 


For the past three years in the month of August, the centre has taken up a collection of school supplies for 
students at the Champlain primary school in the South-Centre area. The centre’s goal is to ensure that all 
children start school with the supplies they need to succeed. It also aims to make life easier for numerous 
parents who find the back-to-school season a real financial drain. The arrival of spring marks the beginning 
of the Easter collection. This year, every child received a book, along with a tasty chocolate Easter egg 
courtesy of the Club Richelieu. 


Life in the heart of centres 


Street youth make people feel uncomfortable, and their parents draw a lot of criticism. To break down 
prejudices and show what families of runaway teens experience, the Guy-Favreau YMCA and Parents en marge 
de la rue organized a photo exhibition called Emotions noir sur blanc. The exhibition, which was produced by 
four mothers of street children, was a resounding success and portrayed a little-known viewpoint on the issue. 


The centre also donated a computer to the Eugenio Aguilar Trigueros school in Canton Los Lagartos, El 
Salvador. The delivery of this essential learning tool was cause for celebration at the school. 


HOCHELAGA-MAISONNEUVE YMCA - ERIC TOUSIGNANT — 
15 YEARS OLD AND BRIMMING WITH IDEAS 

After attending the Glocal Forum in Rome on the role of urban centres in the broader context of globalization, 
Eric, a member of the Hochelaga-Maisonneuve YMCA, felt inspired to sign on as a volunteer at the centre’s 
day camp in Summer 2002. In the fall of the same year, he set up an Introduction to Computers workshop for 
children in the Between School and Home program, organized sports activities and assisted Help with 
Homework monitors. At the same time, Eric attended the Young Leaders Club where he organized a murder 
mystery night for teens and lent a helping hand to the Young Explorers program facilitator on weekends. His 
recent participation in our canoe/camping trip gave him the idea to organize a bike tour next year for youth 
aged 13 to 17. 


In Spring 2003, Eric was elected Volunteer of the Week in the Helping Neighbour contest on the Village2Online 
community portal. Eric is living proof that there’s nothing like the overflowing energy of youth. 


YMCA KAMP KANAWANA - DEFINING SPIRIT AND LEADERSHIP FOR OVER 100 YEARS 
Although this respected institution is more than 100 years old, its dynamic style and leadership role are the 
envy of many a younger institution. 


Registration has increased 40% over the past three years. This summer, 60 youth explored our challenging 
rivers and trails. On site at Kamp Kanawana, 770 Kampers enjoyed a whole range of outdoor activities in the 
same spirit of fun and togetherness as the first Kampers in 1894. 


This summer, we upgraded a number of our facilities and programs, established a new Local Advisory Council 
to conduct safety audits, and welcomed one of the most mature and culturally diverse groups of counselors 
and program staff ever. 


The Kamp’s summer staff founded a volunteer group called Non Nobis Solum (Kanawana’s motto, which means 
“not for ourselves alone”) whose goal is to organize community outreach projects and raise funds to sponsor 
youth in our partner YMCA in Haiti. 


Kamp Kanawana also organized off-season programming, especially during winter and spring break weeks. In 
addition, it is planning to launch several new programs, including: 3-day Family Kamp, adventure trips for 
teens, leadership workshops in Montreal-area schools, etc.

Life in the heart of centres 


NOTRE-DAME-DE-GRACE YMCA - BIGGER, BETTER AND MORE BEAUTIFUL THAN EVER 
For several years now, the NDG YMCA has organized two major events: Black History Month and March 
Madness. 


To celebrate the 5th anniversary of Black History Month, the centre pulled out all the stops to show the 
diversity of black culture with four introductory-level cooking nights, a variety show, and a special screening 
of the film Hurricane Carter, followed by an autograph session with Lesra Martin who was instrumental in free- 
ing Hurricane Carter. Youth also produced a mural on the great accomplishments that have marked black 
history. The already popular event saw a 20% increase in participation and sponsorship this year. 


The March Madness amateur basketball tournament was such a resounding success that when it came time for 
the finals, the NDG YMCA had to borrow the facilities at LCC, a local high school. Despite the additional space, 
some spectators had to be turned away. This year, 28 teams faced off in a friendly and fun atmosphere. 


These two activities play a key role in making youth in the community proud of who they are and what they 
do. 


POINTE-SAINT-CHARLES YMCA - BIRDS OF PREY DAY 

On June 4, 2003 youth had a day off from the Pointe-St-Charles YMCA’s Help with Homework Club. They went 
to Saint-Jude, near Saint-Hyacinthe, to visit UQROP — a Quebec organization for the rehabilitation of birds 
of prey. During the Chouette a voir activity, youth saw eagles, owls, snowy owls, barn owls, red-tailed hawks 
and other birds of prey in action and in the aviaries. They even saw the birds swallow a few small mice! The 
youth were so spellbound by the presentation that they did not want to leave. Hunger finally got the better 
of them. 


The outing was the culmination of a year’s efforts on the part of some twenty youth from Saint-Gabriel, 
Westmount, FACE and Riverview schools who participate in the Help with Homework program. The day trip fell 
under the personal enrichment aspect of the program, which is aimed at stimulating the students’ curiosity 
and motivation to learn. The Royal Bank and The McConnell Foundation finance the entire program. 


SAINT-LAURENT YMCA - LEADERSHIP SKILLS FOR YOUTH 

The aim of this Saint-Laurent YMCA program is to foster the development of psychosocial skills among youth 
aged 10 to 12. The program was implemented at the Enfant-Soleil school, one of the most underprivileged 
schools on the Island of Montreal, which has 700 students from 45 different cultural communities. The 
program is based on an alternative intervention strategy that focuses primarily on volunteering, as well as 
community, cultural and social activities to help youth gain a sense of responsibility, be more active, develop 
their critical thinking, and become more aware of their potential. 


This year, the 30 youth (20 girls and 10 boys) who registered helped distribute food to some 375 students, 
read stories to the younger ones, contributed to school security and guided peers with problems. By setting 
an example and making a social commitment, the youth have a multiplier effect on their peers. 


ee eee 


Life in the heart of centres 


The young leaders also attended a number of workshops (radio, journalism, social communication, peer 
relationships, volunteering, leadership, nutrition, health, etc.) to learn more about themselves. 


The program has a real impact on the youth, their school friends and families, because the youth learn to 
open their eyes to what's going on around them in their community. 


WEST ISLAND YMCA - CONGRATULATIONS TO RECIPIENTS OF THE 2003 

YASMIN MEHERALLY SCHOLARSHIPS 
In 2001, the West Island YMCA created the Yasmin Meherally Memorial Scholarship in memory of a former staff 
member who was deeply committed to international development. She was about to begin working for the 
International Development Research Council when a tragic car accident took her life. 


Erica Reade, a part-time aquatics instructor at the West Island YMCA, is currently studying International 
Development at McGill University. As part of the North-South program at Dawson College, she spent one month 
in Nicaragua. The trip taught her about poverty and inequality, but also about friendship and compassion. 
Upon her return, she knew that she had found her calling. The scholarship will enable Erica to pursue her 
studies. 


Tara Ramiengar is a counselor in the Westmount YMCA’s summer day camp program and an educator with its 
regular preschool program. She has contributed significantly to improving the quality of the program by 
incorporating reading skills and the arts, while maintaining a strong focus physical activity. In September 
2002, Tara began a Certificate in Community Service at Concordia University. She intends to use her 
scholarship to enroll in the Master's of Education and Community Work program to promote literacy among 
children and adults. While she is studying, she will continue the work she started at the Westmount YMCA. 


WESTMOUNT YMCA - ‘ADOPT-A-CAMPER’ CHALLENGE 

On a beautiful Sunday in May, the Westmount YMCA held its first-ever ‘Adopt-a-Camper’ Challenge — a 5 or 
10-km run that brought together more than 500 participants of all ages, shapes and sizes. The event was 
carefully planned by more than 100 of the centre’s volunteers and staff. 


The objectives of the Challenge were two-fold: 
- To provide runners — from beginners to experts — with a chance to test their mettle on 
the winding, picturesque and hilly roads of Westmount. 
- To raise funds to hire ‘companions’ who can help children with special needs at the 
Westmount YMCA summer day camps. 


Over the past few years, the demand from parents for financial assistance to pay for the service has exceeded 
the centre’s available resources - financial and otherwise. Recognizing the importance of an integrated 
program for children with special needs, volunteers, staff and participants managed to raise over $19,000. 
The funding enabled 43 children to benefit from the one-on-one attention they need. 


The first Challenge generated so much enthusiasm that the event is sure to become an annual one. 


Life in the heart of centres 


INTERNATIONAL PROGRAMS - NORTH-SOUTH FRIENDSHIPS 
This year, a number of exchanges further strengthened the friendship and solidarity between the Montreal 
YMCA and its partners in Haiti, Central and South America. 


In July 2002, twelve teenagers from the Hochelaga-Maisonneuve, Westmount and Cobourg, Ontario centres 
realized the goal they had worked toward for several months. Accompanied by six adult leaders, they flew to 
Nicaragua where they were met by 12 youth from the local YMCA/ACJ. They overcame the challenges of 
communicating in three different languages, did community service work, played and talked together for three 
weeks. Upon their return, the youth organized fund-raising activities to help their Nicaraguan friends pay 
them a return visit. 


In November 2002, three representatives visited the new community of Pequeria Inglaterra (Little England) 
in El Salvador, which is home to the survivors of the devastating earthquakes in 2001. They came back with 
a request from the local YMCA to help set up a ludoteca (toy library). After amassing countless games, books 
and toys, they shipped a full container load to El Salvador. 


In February 2003, eight representatives from the Downtown and Saint-Laurent YMCAs, and two from the 
Montreal YMCA’s International Programs visited our partner YMCA/ACJ in Ecuador, marking a successful 


ten-year partnership between the organizations. The visit included a peace vigil 
organized by youth, a tour of the ACJ’s George Williams elementary school, meet- 
ings with community leaders in poor neighbourhoods, discussions with women who 
have benefited from microcredit training, etc. The delegation returned with greater 
awareness of local needs, and with renewed respect for the work of the local YMCA. 


In March, three delegates visited the four YMCA/ACJs in Honduras, which are locat- 
ed in both urban and rural environments. ACJs offer practical programs and servic- 
es to promote equal opportunities for young women and men that will ensure a bet- 
ter future for them. 


Through these exchanges, the Montreal YMCA has renewed its commitment to “Build Strong Kids, Strong 
Families, Strong Communities” both here at home and abroad.

2002-2003 MONTREAL YMCA SOCIAL RESULTS 


In 2002-2003, the Montreal YMCA facilitated access to its programs and services for more than 5,574 people who were in financial 


difficulty. 
Also, through its programs and activities, the Montreal YMCA reached 129,038 people in 2002-2003.

SENIOR MANAGEMENT MONTREAL 
YMCA

The Montreal YMCA Foundation Inc. 


The role of the Foundation is to ensure long-term funding for the Montreal YMCA so all of our 
centres can play a front-line role in the community, while providing access for all to our 
programs. 


To fully achieve its objectives, the Foundation worked to develop an increased presence for 
the YMCA in new communities this year. Some projects are well under way and could be 
implemented in the coming months. 


Another change this year is the adoption of a new support strategy by our endowment fund 
managers. From now on, the endowment fund will finance a smaller number of programs, but 
provide them with increased support so programs have greater impact on their target 
clientele. ; 


The Foundation also continued to prepare for the launching of its next 
fund-raising campaigns in 2004, which include: a major revitalization 
campaign, a planned giving campaign and an endowment fund 
campaign. By managing these various campaigns at the same time, the 
Foundation will be in a better position to respond to the short and 
long-term needs of the Montreal YMCA. 


Much was accomplished, yet there is still so much more to do. We wish to thank our board 
members, Foundation staff and all volunteers, especially those who joined us this year in our 
local and association-based campaign committees. 


Claude A. Garcia Marcel Coté 
Chairman of the Board President

ANNUAL GOLF TOURNAMENT 


The 18" annual Montreal YMCA Golf Tournament, which drew 128 people to the Country Club of Montréal in Saint-Lambert on Monday, June 2, 2003, 
helped raise $52,120. The funds were used to finance several Montreal YMCA youth programs. 


Thank you to the 33 sponsors of our event. 


Thank you to our Patrons of Honour: 
BMO Nesbitt Burns 

Caisse Centrale Desjardins 

Entretien d’immeubles Sermax 
Fasken Martineau Dumoulin 
Langlois Kronstrém Desjardins 

RBC Royal Bank 

RBC Capital Markets 

Samson Bélair / Deloitte & Touche 
Standard Life 


We also wish to thank the numerous individuals and companies that donated door prizes and gifts for the silent auction. 


Our hearfelt thanks to the volunteers who helped make the tournament a great success: 
Laurent Giguére, Claire Lemieux, Jacques Luys and Claire Webster.

ANNUAL CAMPAIGNS 


Thank you to all our donors 


The Montreal YMCA and its Foundation are proud to acknowledge the many individuals, corporations and 
organizations that generously contribute to our revitalization campaign every year, as well as to the local 
campaigns organized by our ten centres and Kamp Kanawana. This year, more than 1,000 individuals and 180 
corporations and foundations donated $145,890 to help the Montreal YMCA build strong kids, strong families 
and strong communities for thousands of children, youth and families. We thank you on their behalf.

Thank you to all our donors 


ENDOWMENT FUND 


The YMCA Endowment Fund was established to ensure long-term support for the Montreal YMCA’s mission of 
community service. Only revenues from the Fund are used to support our various programs. With the current 
donations and planned giving of the 85 Heritage Club members, future generations of Montrealers will con- 
tinue to lead more fulfilling lives through the YMCA. 


We wish to thank the following members of the Heritage Club for their generosity:
